name: Olga Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the copper pit outside town, one of the big ones that carries about 220 tonnes a load. Twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off, and on day shift I'm on the road by 5:20 so I can grab coffee in the crib room before the pre-start meeting. Then it's loop after loop: down the ramp to the shovel, wait while it loads me, back up to the crusher, tip, do it again. I like the quiet up in the cab and I like the crew, but I don't love the dust or the hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Night shift wears me out. My partner Tom drives a school bus, so on my night weeks he does breakfast and the school run for Mei and Jonah, and I barely see them. What keeps me there is the money, honestly, even though I'm on a lower rate than the contractor crews because I came in on a lower grade and never pushed for a move. I'm also on the union site committee, so I feel like I owe the crew something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every year someone from head office shows a slide about the future of mining, and every year I'm still driving the same truck. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union group chat about all the money they wasted on consultants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the thing I worry about isn't the chatbot stuff, it's the driverless trucks, and those are already here at other pits. So even if AI is mostly hype, the company could still bring in autonomous haulage, and then I'm in trouble anyway. Hype or not, it doesn't change my mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up and keep my head down, mostly. I'd stay on the site committee and push for a clause in the next agreement that says no driverless trucks without talks first. And I'd try to put a bit aside each fortnight, but I've said that every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, with a small knot in my stomach. It's the same knot I've had since I first saw a video of a truck with no one in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try to put a bit aside. What usually stops that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something always breaks. Last winter it was the car's gearbox, $1,900, and that wiped out what we had. Before that it was Jonah's braces. There's never a quiet month in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you talk to about the driverless trucks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, our committee rep, mostly. He's been at the pit thirty years and he says they'll never make it work in our wet season, the haul roads turn to soup. I want to believe him, but I've seen the photos from the iron ore mines and those trucks don't seem to mind the mud.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so and joke in the union chat about the money wasted on consultants. Every year there's a slide about the future of mining and I'm still in the same truck.
S0.think: The real threat to me was never chatbots, it's driverless haul trucks, and those exist whether AI is hype or not. So even in this picture my job isn't really safe.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and stays on the union site committee. Pushes for a clause in the next agreement that bans driverless trucks without talks first, and tries again to save a little each fortnight.
S0.feel: Mostly normal, with a small background knot in her stomach about driverless trucks.
S0.quote: Hype or not, it doesn't change my mortgage.
S0.fieldNote: Even in the calmest picture she doesn't relax, because she separates AI hype from robot trucks that already exist elsewhere. Her savings never build because something always breaks, like the $1,900 gearbox. She trusts the union more than any plan of her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union in the room from day one, before a single truck goes driverless. Online I'd share the stories of the miners in other places who lost their jobs to autonomous fleets. I'd be loud about it, because quiet doesn't get you anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think haul truck drivers are first in line. It's the easiest job to automate on a mine, it's just driving in loops. Some of the younger ones might get moved into a control room, but I'm 43 and I've never even used one of those AI apps, so I don't see them picking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every committee meeting and push for a redeployment deal in writing: no forced redundancies, retraining paid by the company, and a decent payout if it comes to that. At home we'd cut the streaming services and the takeaway on Fridays. I'd also ring our local member of parliament's office, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. It feels like being told the date of something bad but not the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used AI apps. If the company offered training in the control room, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say no, and I know how that sounds. I like being in the cab, I like the feel of the truck, and I'm not good at screens. Mei does her homework with one of those chat things and I don't trust it. I'd rather fight for the jobs we've got than pretend I'm going to become a computer person at 43.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mei and Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mum's job might change but we'll be all right, which is a half-lie. Mei is 12 and she'd see through it. She'd ask if we have to sell the house, and I wouldn't know what to say.

S1.say: She'd say the union needs to be in the room from day one before any truck goes driverless. Online she'd share stories of miners elsewhere who lost jobs to autonomous fleets.
S1.think: Haul truck drivers are first in line because driving loops is the easiest thing to automate. At 43 with no interest in screens or AI, she doesn't think she'd be picked for the control room.
S1.do: Pushes through the union committee for a written deal with no forced redundancies and paid retraining. Cuts streaming services and Friday takeaway, and contacts her local member of parliament for the first time.
S1.feel: Tight in the chest, like knowing something bad is coming without knowing when.
S1.quote: I'd rather fight for the jobs we've got than pretend I'm going to become a computer person at 43.
S1.fieldNote: She wants the company to pay for retraining but admits she probably wouldn't take it. That contradiction doesn't bother her much; for her the fight itself is the plan. The question about her daughter hit hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the bosses' dream come true and the rest of us are being thrown away. I'd be at every rally, and I'd say it online too, that the government needs to step in now, not after the pit is empty. If robots can do everything, someone has to make the owners share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it means I'm out of work inside a year and there's nothing else for me here. The only other big employer in town is the hospital and they'd be automating too. With less than a month of money saved, two years is nothing. We'd be behind on the mortgage by the second month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd do is ring the bank and ask about hardship arrangements before we miss a payment. I'd apply for every bit of government support going, and I'd ask Tom's sister if we could stay with her in the city if it came to that. I'd keep going to the union, but I'd know it wasn't enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like falling with nothing to grab. I'd be awake at three in the morning running numbers that don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do in those two years before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much that would matter, if I'm honest. I'd work every overtime shift they offered to scrape together a few thousand. I wouldn't start a course, because what would I train for that a robot couldn't do by 2028? I'd just try to have some cash in a jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, probably, because the mortgage has to come first. Then the power bill, and I'd ring them and beg. I've seen my mother do that, ringing the power company with a cup of tea going cold, and I swore I wouldn't.

S2.say: She'd call it the bosses' dream come true and go to every rally. She'd say online that government must step in now and make owners share the gains.
S2.think: She expects to be out of work within a year with nothing else in town, and to fall behind on the mortgage by the second month. Two years of warning is too little to matter.
S2.do: Calls the bank about hardship arrangements before missing payments and applies for every government support. Works all overtime in the two years beforehand, keeps up union rallies and asks her partner's sister about staying in the city.
S2.feel: Like falling with nothing to grab, awake at three in the morning running numbers that don't work.
S2.quote: I've seen my mother do that, ringing the power company with a cup of tea going cold, and I swore I wouldn't.
S2.fieldNote: Two years feels like no time at all to her; she can't name anything worth training for. Her plan is about surviving the bills, not changing course. The memory of her mother on the phone to the power company carried more weight than anything she said about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say the government has to act, but with five years I'd say there's no excuse for them not to. I'd push for a law that makes companies pay into a fund for every worker a robot replaces. I'd say it on the union page and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think five years just means I watch it coming for longer. I'd be 48 when it lands, which is too old to start again and too young to stop. It doesn't save my job, it just gives me time to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few years I'd try to pay down the car loan so there's one less bill when the end comes. I'd stand for union delegate, which I've avoided, because someone has to bargain the exit terms. Once it arrived I'd lean on whatever the government had set up and on Tom's bus wage until that went too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy and slow, like a long drive in fog. Not the panic of the fast one, but a weight that doesn't lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A payout, maybe, if we bargain hard. Five years is enough time to win something in an agreement. Two years isn't. So for me the extra time is about the union, not about me learning anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's too late to start again. Is there anything you'd consider learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something in the care side, like aged care, because I looked after my dad at the end. But even that, the card says robots do hands-on work too. I keep running into the same wall.

S3.say: She'd say five years leaves government with no excuse, and push for a law making companies pay into a fund for each replaced worker. She'd say it on the union page and at the pub.
S3.think: Five years just stretches out the worry. At 48 she'd be too old to start again and too young to stop, so the extra time doesn't save her job.
S3.do: Pays down the car loan over the first years and stands for union delegate to bargain exit terms. Once it arrives she relies on government support and her partner's wage while it lasts.
S3.feel: Heavy and slow, like a long drive in fog, without the panic of the fast version.
S3.quote: I'd be 48 when it lands, which is too old to start again and too young to stop.
S3.fieldNote: For her the extra time is useful only for bargaining, not for personal change. She briefly considered aged care, drawing on caring for her father, then talked herself out of it. Her focus stays on collective deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it like we waste everything else. I'd want a proper plan for mining towns, written with the workers, not handed down. And I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years puts me at 53 when it lands. That's close enough to the end of the mortgage that maybe, with a payout and Tom's wage, we could hang on. It's still bad, but it's bad I can almost see around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first few years I'd try to get the mortgage down by putting overtime straight onto it. I'd push hard in the union for early retirement terms for anyone over 50 when the trucks go. And I'd sit down with Mei and Jonah about what they study, because I don't want them coming to the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still, but with a little room to breathe. Less like falling and more like a long climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where you talk to people, like nursing or teaching, but I don't know if that's safe either by then. Mostly I'd tell them to leave town. That's hard to say out loud, because this town is everything I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said each time you won't retrain. With ten years, does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If the union got a proper course, at the pit, in work hours, with people I know, I might do it. I won't go sit in a classroom in the city with a bunch of twenty-year-olds. That's just me.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a gift that mustn't be wasted, and call for a plan for mining towns written with workers. She'd tell anyone who would listen.
S4.think: She'd be 53 when it lands, close enough to the end of the mortgage that a payout and her partner's wage might carry them. It's still bad, but she can almost see around it.
S4.do: Puts overtime straight onto the mortgage over the first years and pushes the union for early retirement terms for over-50s. Talks with her kids about studying something that keeps them away from the pit.
S4.feel: Still worried, but with room to breathe; more like a long climb than a fall.
S4.quote: Mostly I'd tell them to leave town. That's hard to say out loud, because this town is everything I know.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years softens her only a little, because her plan still relies on a payout and her partner's job. She opened up slightly to retraining if it came through the union, at the pit, with people she knows. Telling her children to leave town was the hardest thing she said.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. We've got no cushion, so it would knock us flat in a couple of months. What would help is a guarantee from government that if robots take the jobs, the money they save goes back to the people and towns that lost them, plus a pause on mortgage payments for workers who are laid off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. When the pit cuts shifts, the bakery on Ridge Street cuts hours, and the footy club loses sponsors. It's never just the miners. I'd want people to remember that.

headlineQuote: When the pit cuts shifts, the bakery on Ridge Street cuts hours, and the footy club loses sponsors. It's never just the miners.
portrait: Olga Chen is a 43-year-old haul truck driver at a copper pit, with a bus-driver partner, two kids, a mortgage and almost nothing saved. She is a committed union member who sees the fight for a fair deal as her main plan, and she says plainly that she won't retrain to work with screens. Even the hype scenario leaves her uneasy, because driverless trucks already exist. The two-year AGI picture leaves her panicked about the bills, while extra years mostly matter to her as time for the union to bargain exit terms and for her to pay down debt.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because with no cushion her family would be knocked flat within a couple of months.
whatWouldHelp: A government guarantee that money saved by robots goes back to the workers and towns that lost jobs, and a pause on mortgage payments for laid-off workers.
